blocks.text: Progress Report: Stormwater Management Plan

We are at the midpoint of the stormwater management plan for Johnson PLC, and the work is on schedule and within budget. This report sets out where the plan stands, what we completed since we began, what the second half holds, and the few items worth keeping an eye on. Nothing here calls for a decision from you today; it is a picture of steady progress.
Where we stand

The plan for {{fact:f:E-2004-001.client}} is roughly half complete. The existing conditions are set, the drainage areas are confirmed against the survey, and the hydrologic and hydraulic model is built and running. We have moved out of analysis and into the design of the detention and water quality facilities.

The work is tracking with our costs. We remain within the fixed fee of {{fact:f:E-2004-001.fee}} for the engagement, and we see nothing in the second half that would change that. No additional scope has been requested, and the design has not grown beyond what we agreed to prepare.

We are also keeping the reviewing agency in mind as we design, not only at submission. Pamela Warren has taken plans through this authority before, and she is shaping the detention and water quality design to what it expects. That is the surest way to clear the first round of comments without a redesign.
What we finished this period

Charles Olson set the existing-conditions base and reconciled the drainage areas against the survey. One low point at the property line drains off the site, and we chose to carry that flow in the model rather than assume it away. That keeps the design honest and avoids a surprise in review.

Pamela Warren built the model and produced the preliminary runoff figures. The required release rates follow the regional water authority's standards, and the detention basin is sized to meet them. The water quality measure will sit at the basin outlet, where it does the most good with the least added structure.

Jeffrey Perez found a conflict between a proposed storm line and an existing utility, and he has resolved it and is turning the affected sheets. We have asked the owner for the record utility drawings so we can confirm what is actually in the ground before we commit the line.

Across the period the three of us worked from the same design memoranda, so the sheets, the model, and the base all tell one story. Small as that sounds, it is what keeps a plan set clean under a careful review.

We also looked ahead to the outfall, where the basin discharges. The receiving channel can take the controlled flow, and we will protect the outlet against scour. Settling that now keeps it from becoming a comment later, when it is harder to fix.
What comes next
In the second half we complete the detention and water quality design and set the final grading. Pamela Warren will lock the model once the grading is fixed, since the two depend on each other.

Jeffrey Perez will draft the plan set from the completed design, and Charles Olson will keep the base sheet current as the design settles. We will bring the design to you for a review before anything is finalized.
We would like to hold that design review in the coming weeks, once the grading is set. We will propose a time that suits you and walk the plan with you in person.

After that review we assemble the plan set and the supporting calculations, and we prepare the submission to the regional water authority. Our fee covers one round of response to the agency's comments, and we have held time for it.

None of the second half depends on new information from you beyond the utility records already requested. That is the position we wanted to be in at the midpoint. It means the schedule is in our hands, and we intend to keep it there.
Items to watch

Two items could affect the schedule, and neither is serious today. The first is the record utility information. Until we have it, the storm line design carries an assumption we would prefer to confirm before we build on it.

The second is the grading. The detention sizing depends on it, so a late change to the grading would ripple into the basin design. We are holding the drafting until the grading is set, which keeps that risk small and avoids redrawing sheets.
In summary
We are at the midpoint, on schedule, and within the fee. The path to a submittable plan is clear, and the open items are ordinary ones we can close.
We will bring the design to you at the review before it is finalized. Prepared by Charles Olson, Design Technician.
